findings.title: Stripe webhook at POST /webhooks/stripe marks orders paid without verifying the Stripe signature

verification.reasoning: api/webhooks.js:11-16 calls JSON.parse(req.body.toString()) and then runs the 'paid' update and the enqueue. It never reads the stripe-signature header or calls constructEvent, and the Stripe client built at :8 is never used. src/config.js:5-8 and .env.example:1-3 define no webhook secret. src/server.js:10 registers app.use(express.json()) before the /webhooks mount at :16, and the mount has no auth middleware (unlike :13-15). express.json therefore parses the body first, and the route's express.raw then skips it as already parsed. body-parser's strict mode accepts arrays, so a body like ["{...event...}"] arrives as an array whose toString() is the inner string, which then parses into an attacker-chosen event. Even without the array trick, nothing authenticates the endpoint. A real Stripe object body becomes "[object Object]" and throws inside an async Express 4 handler, so the reporter's side note about lost legitimate payments also holds. I did not run the exploit; the static path is enough for critical.

findings.rationale: The handler calls JSON.parse on the request body and then runs `update orders set status = 'paid'` using event.data.object.metadata.orderId. It never reads the stripe-signature header or calls stripe.webhooks.constructEvent. The Stripe client built on line 8 is never used, and config/.env.example define no webhook signing secret. The global express.json() at server.js:10 runs before the route's express.raw, so req.body is already parsed. A JSON array whose only element is the event serialized as a string gets through: Array.prototype.toString returns that string, so JSON.parse works and any caller can mark any order paid. I worked this out from body-parser behavior and did not run it.

evidence.codeSnippet: const stripe = new Stripe(config.stripeKey);
app.use(express.json());
app.use('/webhooks', webhooks);

findings.impact: An unauthenticated attacker can mark any pending order as paid and trigger a receipt email without paying, so goods ship for free. Real Stripe deliveries are object bodies. For those, req.body.toString() returns "[object Object]" and JSON.parse throws inside an async Express 4 handler, which leaves an unhandled rejection (on Node 20, used in CI, this exits the process by default). Real payments are probably never recorded, but a run is needed to confirm that.

recommendation.action: Mount the webhook router ahead of app.use(express.json()) so express.raw gets the untouched bytes. Add STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET to config. Build the event with stripe.webhooks.constructEvent(req.body, req.headers['stripe-signature'], secret) and return 400 on failure, before any parsing or database write. Wrap the handler in try/catch or pass errors to next(err).

verification.reasoning: The defect is real. api/orders.js:20 inserts the order and api/orders.js:21-23 inserts each item with a separate db.query call. src/db.js:8 runs each call as pool.query, which autocommits, and there is no BEGIN/COMMIT anywhere in the repo. evidence.codeSnippet: res.status(500).json({ error: error.message, stack: error.stack });

findings.impact: Clients and monitoring see 5xx for bad input, so error alerts are noisy and clients cannot tell their mistakes from outages.

findings.title: CI step echoes STRIPE_SECRET_KEY into the workflow log

verification.reasoning: The pattern is real. .github/workflows/ci.yml:12-13 maps secrets.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY into env and echoes it. But the claimed exposure is overstated in two ways. First, the value is echoed raw with no transformation. GitHub Actions automatically redacts registered secrets that appear verbatim in logs, so the log shows *** and not the key. The masking gap the reporter mentions applies only to transformed values, and there are none here. Second, the step never runs today. It comes after `run: npm ci` at ci.yml:10, which fails without a lockfile (no package-lock.json in git ls-files; see index 1), and a failed step stops the job. The trigger is `on: [push]` (ci.yml:2), so only people with push access can start a run, and they could already add a workflow that reads the secret. This is a hygiene problem: a fake deploy step should not handle the secret at all. It is not a critical key leak.

findings.rationale: The step maps secrets.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY into env and then runs echo with the variable interpolated. The value is written to the job log. GitHub masking only matches the exact string, so any transformation of the value would not be masked.

evidence.codeSnippet:
- run: echo "Deploying with key $STRIPE_SECRET_KEY"
        env: { STRIPE_SECRET_KEY: "${{ secrets.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY }}" }

findings.impact: The Stripe secret key is exposed to anyone who can read the Actions logs or artifacts. It is also exposed to anyone who can trigger runs on pushed branches. The key can be used to charge, refund, or read customer data.

recommendation.action: Delete the echo step and the secret env mapping. If a real deploy step is added later, pass the secret only to that step and never print it. Rotate the Stripe key because it has already been logged.

findings.title: Mail-provider fetch in sendReceipt has no explicit timeout

verification.reasoning: workers/email.js:7-11 calls fetch with no signal, so on Node 20 (ci.yml:9) only undici's defaults bound it. The Worker at workers/email.js:18 sets no concurrency, so it runs one job at a time and a hung call blocks the queue. Only the headers timeout matters here, because the response body is never read (only response.ok at :12). Low severity is appropriate, especially since the worker's deployment is not shown in the repo.

findings.rationale: The fetch to api.mailprovider.example passes no AbortSignal. Only Node/undici's default headers and body timeouts (about 300s each) bound it. The Worker uses the default concurrency of 1, so one hung provider call holds up every queued receipt for several minutes.
findings.impact: When the mail provider degrades, the receipt queue stalls for minutes per job instead of failing fast and retrying.

recommendation.action: Pass signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000) to the fetch, and let the resulting error fail the job so the BullMQ retry policy handles it.
recommendation.code_example: await fetch(url, { method: 'POST', headers, body, signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000) });

findings.title: Poller tick has no error handling, so a DB error crashes the process or stops polling

verification.reasoning: src/poller.js:11 passes the async tick to setInterval with no catch. src/poller.js:6 is an await db.query with no try/catch, so a DB error becomes an unhandled rejection that kills the process on Node 15+. With pollIntervalMs at 500 (src/config.js:7), slow queries can make ticks overlap. The script only runs when executed directly (src/poller.js:10), and the grep found no other module importing it, so the impact is limited to a dev script. Low is correct.

findings.rationale: setInterval calls the async tick every 500ms with no catch. A rejected db.query is an unhandled rejection. Ticks also overlap if a query takes longer than the interval.

evidence.codeSnippet: setInterval(tick, config.pollIntervalMs);

findings.impact: The dev dashboard script dies on the first transient DB error. It is a manual script, so impact is limited.

recommendation.action: Wrap tick in try/catch, or use a self-rescheduling setTimeout so ticks cannot overlap.

findings.title: Schema is a single unversioned schema.sql with no migration history

verification.reasoning: The only schema artifact is prisma/schema.sql:1-23, written as plain CREATE TABLE statements. git ls-files shows no migrations directory. package.json:5-6 has no migration tool or script, and .github/workflows/ci.yml:10-12 applies no schema. There is no versioned path to an existing database. Low severity is accurate.

findings.rationale: The schema lives only in prisma/schema.sql, as plain create table statements. No migrations directory or tool is present, and no ORM is in use. The file cannot be applied incrementally or reproducibly to an existing database.

evidence.codeSnippet:
create table users (

findings.impact: Schema changes such as the indexes and constraints above have no safe, ordered path to production. Environments can drift apart.

recommendation.action: Adopt a versioned migration tool such as node-pg-migrate or dbmate, and move this file into an initial migration.

systemicPatterns.name: Untrusted Boundaries
systemicPatterns.description: Request input reaches SQL, the shell, and payment state without validation or authentication. Route params and body keys are interpolated into SQL, a body field is passed to a shell, the Stripe webhook is accepted unsigned, and client-supplied prices become order totals. Authorization is applied at the router level only, so routes under /api/users never check ownership or role.

PATCH /api/users/:id builds the SET clause from request body keys
POST /api/admin/export passes req.body.table into a shell command
Stripe webhook at POST /webhooks/stripe marks orders paid without verifying the Stripe signature
PATCH /api/users/:id lets a user set their own role to admin
POST /api/orders takes the order total from client-supplied priceCents
GET /api/users/:id returns any user's record without an ownership check
GET /api/users returns every user's email and role to any logged-in user
systemicPatterns.recommendation: Parameterize every query and allowlist identifiers (columns, table names). Verify the Stripe signature with the raw body mounted before express.json. Add per-route ownership and role checks, and compute prices server-side.

systemicPatterns.name: Insecure Defaults
systemicPatterns.description: Secrets have committed fallbacks. The Stripe key and JWT secret both default to literals in src/config.js, .env.example ships the same JWT value, and the CI workflow hands the Stripe secret to a placeholder deploy step. A deployment with a missing env var runs silently with known secrets instead of failing.
contributing_findings: JWT secret falls back to 'change-me'
Live-format Stripe secret key hardcoded as config fallback
CI step echoes STRIPE_SECRET_KEY into the workflow log
systemicPatterns.recommendation: Make config fail at startup when a required secret is missing. Remove every literal fallback and strip the secret from the CI echo step.

systemicPatterns.name: No Safety Net
systemicPatterns.description: Nothing catches regressions or runtime faults. The only test compares a literal to itself, no linter runs, CI cannot pass because npm ci has no lockfile, and Express 4 async handlers have no error wrapper, so a single bad request crashes the process.
contributing_findings: The only test, 'health shape', compares a literal to an identical literal and can never fail
Stripe webhook handler, which marks orders paid and enqueues receipts, has no tests
No linter, formatter or type checker is configured or run in CI
No lockfile is tracked, so the CI `npm ci` step fails and production dependencies are unpinned
Async Express 4 handlers have no wrapper, so DB errors and validation throws become unhandled rejections
systemicPatterns.recommendation: Commit the lockfile, wrap async handlers (or move to Express 5), add ESLint to CI, and replace the placeholder test with route tests for health, auth, orders and the webhook.

systemicPatterns.name: Happy Path Only
systemicPatterns.description: Failure and shutdown paths are not designed. Order creation runs as separate autocommit statements, the email worker swallows provider errors and has no timeout, webhook redelivery is not deduplicated, the process has no SIGTERM handling, and the error handler leaks stacks while ignoring err.status.
contributing_findings: POST /api/orders inserts the order and its items as separate autocommit statements
sendReceipt logs mail-provider failures and returns, so BullMQ marks failed receipts as completed
Mail-provider fetch in sendReceipt has no explicit timeout
Stripe webhook redelivery enqueues a duplicate receipt email
Server has no SIGTERM handler and never closes the HTTP server, pg pool or BullMQ queue
Global error handler returns error.message and stack trace to clients
Validation errors tagged status 400 are returned as 500 because the error handler ignores err.status
Poller tick has no error handling, so a DB error crashes the process or stops polling
systemicPatterns.recommendation: Wrap multi-statement writes in a transaction, throw on provider errors so BullMQ retries, add fetch timeouts and event-id dedupe, add graceful shutdown, and return generic errors with the right status.

topFixes.title: GET /api/users/:id interpolates req.params.id into SQL
topFixes.rationale: req.params.id is placed into the query string with a template literal and passed to db.query with no params array. db.query (src/db.js:7-9) forwards the text to pool.query unchanged. Any authenticated user reaches this route; requireAuth is the only guard (src/server.js:13).

topFixes.title: PATCH /api/users/:id builds the SET clause from request body keys
topFixes.rationale: Object.keys(req.body) are placed into the SQL text verbatim as column names. Values are parameterized, but identifiers are not checked against an allowlist. The only guard is that the caller is patching their own id, and any authenticated user meets that.

topFixes.title: Stripe webhook at POST /webhooks/stripe marks orders paid without verifying the Stripe signature
topFixes.rationale: The handler calls JSON.parse on the request body and then runs `update orders set status = 'paid'` using event.data.object.metadata.orderId. It never reads the stripe-signature header or calls stripe.webhooks.constructEvent. The Stripe client built on line 8 is never used, and config/.env.example define no webhook signing secret. The global express.json() at server.js:10 runs before the route's express.raw, so req.body is already parsed. A JSON array whose only element is the event serialized as a string gets through: Array.prototype.toString returns that string, so JSON.parse works and any caller can mark any order paid. I worked this out from body-parser behavior and did not run it.
